body: Indonesia's license plates are black with white letters, with newer plates sometimes being white. In Indonesia, commercial vehicles use yellow plates.
Driving side in Indonesia is on the left. Malaysia also drives left, but the Philippines drives on the right.
Indonesia uses white and yellow road center lines, with outer lines always white. Yellow center lines are more common recently.
Poles in Indonesia are mainly round, made of steel or concrete, often painted black and featuring the Indonesian flag colors.
Indonesia frequently uses black-and-white or yellow-and-black bollards; UK-style bollards are mostly in Kalimantan.
Waystones in Indonesia are usually yellow, angled towards the road, and have city/town abbreviations, with the largest on top.
Indonesian language resembles Malaysian but influenced by Dutch. Examples include 'televisi' vs. 'televisyen'.
Red and white banners are widespread across Indonesia, with more colorful flags occasionally displayed.
Cigarette ads, often in black or red, feature graphics and are around 18,000 Rp; look for the word 'PERINGATAN'.
In Indonesia, motorcycles have front license plates, unlike most Southeast Asian countries.
The official currency of Indonesia is the Rupiah (Rp).
Coverage in Indonesia is limited, especially outside Java, Papua, Kalimantan, Aceh, and parts of Sulawesi and North Maluku.
Across Indonesia, administrative divisions called 'Kabupaten' or regencies are marked on signs and billboards; there are 417 of them.
Many addresses show cardinal directions: North=Utara, East=Timur, South=Selatan, West=Barat, Central=Tengah.
Indonesia features even and uneven pole tops, indicating regional pole styles and aiding in region guessing.
Triangle attachments on pole tops are specific to certain regions, not on stacked poles.
Trident-style pole tops are mainly in Central Java and Yogyakarta, less in South and West Kalimantan and North Sumatra.
Bali features both even and uneven poles, including unique rectangular pole tops.
On the Lesser Sunda Islands, poles with an extra long support on the top, sometimes with two supports.
North and Central Sulawesi, Gorontalo, have poles with an extra attachment below the horizontal bar.
On the east coast of Central Sulawesi, thin black poles with light blue and green tapes near the top are common, rarely seen in north Southeast Sulawesi.
These poles are mostly in North Sumatra, with insulators featuring an uneven bar and one or two insulators on each side.
Satellite dishes indicate whether you're north or south of the equator; level dishes suggest proximity.
In Central Sulawesi, poles have black bottoms, white midsections, and yellow tops.
Fences in Sulawesi are mainly white with accents of blue or red.
Green paint on bridge sides is typical in South and Central Kalimantan.
Oil palm plantations are mainly in Sumatra and Kalimantan, rarely in Sulawesi.
Most rice farming occurs on Java, with lesser spots in South Sulawesi and South Sumatra.
The Nusas are drier, less lush, especially in the east, with less foliage and brown terrain.
North Sumba may feature sparse savannah, especially in Generation 3 coverage, always with white cars.
Red soil often appears in Batam and the Bangka Belitung islands east of Sumatra.
Tile roofs are most typical in Java, with variations in South Kalimantan and South Sumatra, often flatter.
Sheet metal roofs dominate in northern Indonesia where tiles are rare, especially in Kalimantan, Sulawesi, and Sumatra.
Gable roofs with horns are common in South Sulawesi, Riau, and parts of Kalimantan, often with Bugis houses.
Toraja houses in South Sulawesi have saddle-shaped roofs and are elevated from the ground.
